## About "Hydras of the World"

The main objective of this project is to provide a comprehensive resource for anyone interested in the global diversity of Hydra. Understanding this diversity within an evolutionary framework is essential for researchers working with the genus. While modern biology has made remarkable progress by focusing on standard model organisms, an overwhelming skew toward a tiny handful of species creates a severely distorted view of life—a distinct taxonomic bias.

Hydra researchers often describe their study subjects as "non-model organisms," yet they frequently generalize findings based on a single laboratory strain of sometimes uncertain origin. Variation is the norm, not the exception. While every study obviously cannot include multiple strains or species, these pages aim to encourage colleagues to rigorously characterize the taxonomic status of the strains they study rather than simply reporting a species name without any additional information.

Compounding this issue, evidence shows that standard laboratory strains—such as *Hydra vulgaris 105* and *Hydra vulgaris AEP*—have significantly diverged since being collected and maintained across different laboratories worldwide for over 40 and 30 years, respectively. Very likely, these laboratory cultures regularly experience genetic bottlenecks and artificial selection in captivity. Keep in mind this potential source of variation when reporting work on a given species and strain. 

Understanding the diversity and distribution of Hydra around the world requires a monumental effort, and no one contributed more to this enterprise than **Dr. Richard D. Campbell** at University of California, Irvine.  Campbell collected specimens from approximately 2,000 distinct locations across every unfrozen continent, resolving numerous taxonomic complexities and clarifying the validity of many species (e.g. Campbell 1987, 1989; Campbell & Holstein, 1991; Holstein, Campbell & Tardent, 1990).

Dr. Robert Steele (UCI) and I have completed several collecting trips in search of hydras. I am deeply grateful for Rob's companionship and support, especially in some extraordinary destinations like the Peruvian highlands, the Peruvian Amazon, northern Mexico, the Okefenokee Swamp in Georgia, and the Great Dismal Swamp in Virginia. 
 
More recently, Callen Hyland at the University of San Diego has spearheaded an iNaturalist project to map global observations.
